ILLUSTRATION BY CHUANG ZHAO "Pinocchio Rex" Found; Dinosaur Sported Long Snout Qianzhousaurus sinensis lived alongside its cousin T. rex. By Christine Dell'Amore Published May 9, 2014 • 4 min read It's no lie—a new tyrannosaur nicknamed "Pinocchio rex" has been unearthed in China , a new study says. The discovery confirms that long-snouted tyrannosaurs once roamed the Earth, laying to rest a long-running debate. Formally described as Qianzhousaurus sinensis , the newfound dinosaur had a thin, long nose studded with tiny horns, a far cry from the short, muscular snout of its cousin Tyrannosaurus rex . (Related: " New Pygmy Tyrannosaur Found, Roamed the Arctic .") At about 29 feet (9 meters) long and 1,800 pounds (800 kilograms), the dinosaur was smaller and likely sprightlier than the 42-foot-long (13 meters) T. rex . The two creatures lived side by side about 66 million years ago during the late Cretaceous period , just before the demise of the dinosaurs, according to a study published May 7 in the journal Nature Communications . Scientists happened upon the nearly complete, "one in a million" Qianzhousaurus skeleton at a construction site in Ganzhou (map) , a rapidly developing southern city that's also rich with fossils. pages.title: 'Dueling Dinosaurs' fossil, hidden from science for 14 years, could finally reveal its secrets | National Geographic
pages.description: An exquisitely preserved specimen of a T. rex and Triceratops, tangled together as though they died in combat, has been acquired by a North Carolina museum after more than a decade in private hands.
pages.text: 'Dueling Dinosaurs' fossil, hidden from science for 14 years, could finally reveal its secrets | National Geographic In 2006, commercial fossil hunters found this exquisite, nearly complete tyrannosaur alongside the bones of a plant-eating Triceratops . Now, a North Carolina museum has acquired the prehistoric pair, allowing scientists to begin studying the fossil for the first time. Photograph by Matt Zeher SCIENCE NEWS 'Dueling Dinosaurs' fossil, hidden from science for 14 years, could finally reveal its secrets An exquisitely preserved specimen of a T. rex and Triceratops, tangled together as though they died in combat, has been acquired by a North Carolina museum after more than a decade in private hands. By Michael Greshko Published November 17, 2020 • 11 min read For more than a decade, paleontologists have speculated about a single fossil that preserves skeletons of two of the world’s most famous dinosaurs, Tyrannosaurus rex and Triceratops . Not only are the bones arranged as they once were in life, but the dinosaurs are practically intertwined. Each specimen is among the best of its kind ever found. Together, the pair—nicknamed the “Dueling Dinosaurs”—present a paleontological mystery: Did the beasts just happen to be entombed together by chance, perhaps as carcasses caught on the same river sandbar? Or had they been locked in mortal combat? Nobody has been able to study the fossil to find out. The Dueling Dinosaurs fossil may represent a lethal struggle between a Triceratops and a juvenile T. rex, shown here in this artist's reconstruction of prehistoric Montana.

pages.description: A new campaign encourages visitors to take in the lavish art above their heads at five historic sites across England. There are even cushions for maximum comfort while you gaze
pages.text: 'Lie Down and Look Up' at England's Most Ornate Ceilings, From Sparkling Gold-Leaf Stars to Intricate Plaster Designs at Queen Victoria's Seaside Retreat Skip to main content The Star Chamber inside Bolsover Castle English Heritage Historic buildings across England are encouraging visitors to spend some time considering what often goes over their heads: the oft-forgotten art of ceilings. The conservation charity English Heritage 's “Lie Down and Look Up” campaign, which runs through November 1, highlights five distinctive ceilings across the country. In each room, space has been created and cushions provided to help visitors get as comfortable as possible while looking up—supine if they like—and experience details and craftsmanship they otherwise may have neglected. “Ceilings are often the crowning glory of a historic building. Designed to inspire awe, they can be wonderfully distinctive—with decoration that survives remarkably well,” Jeremy Ashbee, head curator of properties at English Heritage, says in a statement . “But when visiting a historic place, there’s not always the opportunity to enjoy a splendid ceiling to the fullest,” he adds. “We’re inviting visitors to put formality to one side, make themselves at home, linger, even lie down and enjoy the view up above.” One brilliant room, the Star Chamber inside Bolsover Castle in Derbyshire , may give visitors the feeling that they’re actually gazing up at the night sky. pages.description: Some Americans lauded the 30-year-old bank robber as a Robin Hood-esque folk hero. Others castigated him as a violent criminal whose misdeeds were emblematic of the troubled era
pages.text: 'Pretty Boy' Floyd, One of the Most Notorious Outlaws of the Great Depression, Was Shot and Killed in an FBI Raid 92 Years Ago Skip to main content Charles Arthur "Pretty Boy" Floyd was a Depression-era outlaw who earned the title of the nation's "public enemy No. 1." Illustration by Meilan Solly / Images via Bettmann / Getty Images and Newspapers.com It was October 22, 1934. The late afternoon sun baked the Ohio cornfield in a wash of orange and red—an earthly premonition of the bloodshed soon to come. A volley of gunshots cut through the usual autumn quiet as a man in a mud-stained blue suit dashed through the tree line, a group of officers on his tail. Suddenly, he fell. As the officers approached the man, he looked up at them in shock. “I’m done for,” he said . “You’ve hit me twice.” And then—silence. Thirty-year-old Charles Arthur “Pretty Boy” Floyd , America’s public enemy No. 1, was dead at the hands of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Floyd's 1928 prison record Public domain via Wikimedia Commons Nearly a century later, Floyd still captivates the American psyche. One of the most high-profile criminals of the Great Depression—often making headlines alongside the infamous Bonnie Parker and Clyde Barrow , John Dillinger , and George “Machine Gun” Kelly —Floyd is emblematic of his time. A poor American farmer-turned-bootlegger who embraced a life of crime, Floyd danced on the line of lawlessness until he crossed the point of no return. pages.title: 'Wildwood' Is the Longest Stop-Motion Animated Film Ever. Each Frame of the Movie Is a Marvel of Handcrafted World Building
pages.description: Deborah Cook, costumer designer at stop-motion animation studio Laika, discusses creating tiny costumes for puppets in a fantastical world set in the forests of Portland, Oregon
pages.text: 'Wildwood' Is the Longest Stop-Motion Animated Film Ever. Each Frame of the Movie Is a Marvel of Handcrafted World Building Skip to main content Wildwood , the latest film from stop-motion animation studio Laika, features handcrafted sets Courtesy of Laika Wildwood , set in a magical world in the unruly forests bordering Portland, Oregon, is the newest film from animation house Laika . Founded in 2005, the studio became acclaimed for its work on films such as Coraline (2009) and Kubo and the Two Strings (2016). Laika champions practical effects and stop-motion animation —a flipbook-like filmmaking style in which objects are moved frame by frame to create the action seen on screen. At 2 hours and 12 minutes, Wildwood is the longest stop-motion animated film ever made. The story follows the courageous Prue and her classmate Curtis as she embarks on a fantasy adventure in the forests to find her kidnapped baby brother. Costume designer Deborah Cook developed more than 200 pieces for Wildwood . Wildwood - Official Trailer Watch on After her work on Tim Burton’s Corpse Bride , Cook was approached by Laika to work on Coraline . “It was a definite yes,” she says of relocating her life from London to Portland to be part of what would become an Oscar-nominated film . After that production, she stuck with the studio. She was interested in how much Laika’s CEO Travis Knight, who directed Wildwood , was invested in stop-motion. “I really wanted to be part of that,” Cook says. When most people think of traveling to Taiwan, images of breathtaking Sun Moon lake or the towering Taipei 101 skyscraper come to mind. While these destinations are iconic for a reason, there is so much more to discover on the island. In the spirit of Smithsonian magazine's Museum Day , we've assembled ten must-visit museums and historic small towns ⁠—veritable outdoor museums⁠—across Taiwan that offer a window into its diverse cultures, rich history and natural heritage. Whether exploring the world's largest collection of Chinese artifacts in Taipei City or discovering the art of woodcarving in the countryside, Taiwan has something for every cultural traveler. National Palace Museum Modeled after a Chinese imperial palace, the National Palace Museum in Taipei's Shilin District is home to the world's largest collection of Chinese art. Consisting of over 600,000 Chinese art objects, the collection spans five millennia and includes more than 200,000 rare books, 25,000 ceramic pieces and 13,000 jade works. Highlights include an intricately carved jadeite cabbage that dates back to the Qing Dynasty as well as a piece of jasper that bears an uncanny resemblance to a slice of pork belly. pages.description: The LEIA are experimental, county-level estimates of high-speed internet access.
pages.text: 2022 Local Estimates of Internet Adoption (LEIA) 2022 Local Estimates of Internet Adoption (LEIA) Skip Navigation 2022 Local Estimates of Internet Adoption (LEIA) September 09, 2024 The Local Estimates of Internet Adoption (LEIA) is a Census Bureau experimental data product that provides county-level estimates of high-speed internet adoption across the nation. The federal government has created a number of programs meant to improve the availability, adoption, and use of high-speed Internet service, such as the Digital Equity Act programs. Towards this effort, the National Telecommunications and Information Administration has sponsored the Bureau to develop one-year, small area estimates of internet adoption at the county level. The purpose of LEIA is to provide timely and accurate estimates of high-speed internet adoption across the country. We employ 1-year American Community Survey microdata, auxiliary data from the Federal Communications Commission, and small area estimation modeling techniques. 1 This produces reliable estimates of internet adoption for all counties in the United States. Data users can download LEIA data, its feasibility report, and quick guide below. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. 2025 U.S. Energy & Employment Report (USEER) Banner Color Light Text on a Dark Overlay (Default) The U.S. Energy & Employment Report (USEER) provides a comprehensive account of the energy employment landscape across America, including national, state, and county-level energy jobs data. The USEER tracks energy employment across three energy production sectors ( Fuels, Electric Power Generation, and Transmission, Distribution, and Storage ) and two end use sectors ( Energy Efficiency and Motor Vehicles and Component Parts ). This year, the 2025 USEER includes data on wages and employer benefits, allowing policymakers to understand how the U.S. energy sector provides stable, high-paying employment opportunities to hardworking Americans. 2025 USEER & Data 2025 USEER National Report 2025 USEER State Reports 2025 USEER County Data 2025 USEER Appendices 2025 USEER Public Data USEER Background The USEER, as mandated by Congress in 42 USC 18841 , provides a comprehensive account of national, state and county-level energy jobs by industry, technology, and region. Published annually since 2016, the USEER delivers insights into the energy workforce by tracking and reporting of employment within and across key energy sectors.

pages.text: 2026 Census Test: Social Media Toolkit 2026 Census Test: Social Media Toolkit 2026 Census Test: Social Media Toolkit 2026 Census Test: Social Media Toolkit About the 2026 Census Test The 2026 Census Test is the U.S. Census Bureau's first opportunity to try out new tools and methods in two locations in the United States. This operational test, in support of the 2030 Census, will help us improve how we will count everyone in the country in 2030. For the 2026 Census Test, the Census Bureau is also working with the United States Postal Service (USPS) to evaluate ways postal workers may assist with collecting responses from households that do not respond on their own. The 2026 Census Test is the first of two field tests we conduct in preparation for the 2030 Census.
